ddx.step1_summary:
- Chief complaint: 3 days of diarrhoea with central abdominal pain and some vomiting.
- Symptoms: Diarrhoea for ~3 days; frequency very high (needs toilet every ~10 minutes, sensation of incomplete evacuation); central/subumbilical abdominal pain, mild and somewhat relieved by defecation; one episode of vomiting this morning (possibly of fruit); audible bowel sounds; mild abdominal tenderness on palpation. No definite fever reported (patient had some sweating over 4 days but no measured temperature). No visible blood in stool or vomit. Decreased oral intake; reports not drinking much.
- Onset/duration/severity/aggravating-alleviating: Acute onset 3 days ago; persistent, not clearly improving or worsening; aggravated by eating (patient is avoiding food); partially alleviated after toileting (suggests cramping/gas component).
- Past medical history: Asthma. No other chronic illnesses reported.
- Medications/allergies: Uses an inhaler for asthma (recently changed brand/new inhaler). Reports NKDA (no known drug allergies).
- Family/social history: Father died ~10 years ago of bowel (colorectal) cancer. Patient is a 48-year-old male, described as a foreigner; not currently working because of symptoms. No tobacco/alcohol/drug use documented.
- Vital signs/exam findings: No formal vital signs recorded. Exam finding: mild central abdominal tenderness on palpation; otherwise patient ambulant, talking normally, no respiratory distress beyond baseline asthma.
- Labs/imaging: None performed or reported.

(Overall most likely clinical impression in the transcript: acute gastroenteritis / food-borne illness causing diarrhoea, cramping pain, transient vomiting.)

V: Mesenteric ischemia: Acute severe abdominal pain that can present with diarrhoea/ vomiting, but classically severe pain out of proportion to exam — less likely here given subacute diarrhoea and milder tenderness.
Ischemic colitis: Can cause central/left-sided abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea — less likely as patient has no blood and is relatively young without vascular risk factors.
I: Acute viral gastroenteritis (e.g., norovirus, rotavirus): Common cause of acute-onset diarrhoea, vomiting, abdominal cramps lasting 1–7 days — matches 3-day history, frequent stools, cramping relieved by defecation.

Bacterial gastroenteritis / food poisoning (e.g., Salmonella, Campylobacter, Staphylococcal toxin): Can cause more severe cramping, frequent diarrhoea, sometimes vomiting depending on organism; possible if patient ate contaminated food.
Traveller's diarrhoea / enterotoxigenic E. coli: If patient consumed contaminated food/water and is a foreigner or has recent travel/diet change.
N: Colorectal cancer: Family history (father) increases risk; can cause changes in bowel habit and abdominal pain but typically subacute/chronic with weight loss, bleeding — acute 3-day diarrhoea without blood makes this unlikely as the cause of current presentation.
Gastrointestinal malignancy (small bowel tumor): Rarely presents acutely with diarrhoea and cramping; overall low likelihood.
D: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) with diarrhoea-predominant symptoms: Can cause crampy central abdominal pain relieved by defecation and frequent stooling, but IBS is typically chronic/recurrent rather than an acute 3-day illness.
Lactase deficiency / food intolerance: Can produce crampy diarrhoea after specific foods (e.g., dairy) but usually related temporally to ingestion of trigger foods.
I2: Food or chemical toxin ingestion (e.g., food poisoning, preformed toxins like S. aureus or Bacillus cereus): Causes acute onset vomiting/diarrhoea after eating contaminated food; plausible given acute time course.
Medication-related GI upset (new inhaler excipient or systemic side effect): Unlikely — inhalers rarely cause this pattern of diarrhoea, but patient noted a new inhaler.
C: Congenital malrotation or chronic anatomic abnormality: Would usually present earlier in life and/or with different chronicity; unlikely to explain an acute 3-day diarrhoeal illness.
A: Allergic gastroenteritis / food allergy (IgE or non-IgE mediated): Can cause vomiting/diarrhoea after exposure to a specific food (e.g., fruit), but typically associated with other allergic signs (urticaria, angioedema) which are not reported.
T: Intra-abdominal injury/trauma: No history of trauma; unlikely.
E: Endocrine/metabolic causes (hyperthyroidism, adrenal insufficiency): Can cause diarrhoea but would usually have systemic features (weight loss, palpitations, hypotension) absent here.
Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA): Can cause vomiting and abdominal pain, but no history of diabetes or other supportive signs.

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Fits the acute 3-day history of watery diarrhoea, crampy central abdominal pain, one episode of vomiting, frequent bowel motions, relative lack of systemic toxicity or severe focal abdominal signs. Viral agents (norovirus, rotavirus, etc.) commonly cause this pattern and duration.
supporting_evidence: Crampy central abdominal pain relieved somewhat by defecation
One episode of vomiting, decreased appetite, audible bowel sounds
No blood in stool and patient not systemically very unwell
opposing_evidence: Patient reports sweating (uncertain) but no documented fever — though viruses often cause fever, absence does not exclude viral gastroenteritis
High frequency of stooling (~every 10 minutes) is relatively severe but can occur with some bacterial pathogens as well

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Acute diarrhoea and cramping with vomiting can also be caused by bacterial pathogens or preformed toxins. Bacterial causes may produce more severe cramping and frequent stools; lack of fever or blood makes some bacterial etiologies less likely but bacterial infection remains plausible depending on exposures.
supporting_evidence: Acute course (3 days) with high stool frequency and cramping
Vomiting and recent meal (patient had fruit) — possible contaminated food exposure
Patient reports not feeling improved over days
opposing_evidence: No reported fever, no bloody diarrhoea, and no systemic toxicity documented
No history of recent antibiotic use (which would raise risk for C. difficile)

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Irritable bowel syndrome (diarrhoea-predominant) or functional diarrhoea
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: The pattern of central crampy pain relieved by defecation and frequent stooling resembles IBS, but the acute 3-day duration and severity requiring constant toilet access make a new infectious cause more likely. If symptoms recur or become chronic, IBS would be higher on the list.
supporting_evidence: Crampy central pain that is somewhat relieved by bowel movements
Sensation of needing to go again after finishing (tenesmus-like sensation)
opposing_evidence: Symptoms are acute in onset over days rather than chronic/recurrent which is typical for IBS
Associated transient vomiting is less characteristic of IBS

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Medication reaction / iatrogenic (inhaler or new excipient) or toxin ingestion
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Patient is concerned a new inhaler could be responsible, but inhalers rarely produce prominent diarrhoea and vomiting. Food toxin ingestion (preformed toxins) remains a plausible iatrogenic/toxic cause but is grouped with bacterial/food poisoning above.
supporting_evidence: Patient recently started a new inhaler brand and is concerned about it
Acute onset symptoms could theoretically follow exposure to a toxin or contaminant
opposing_evidence: Inhaler side effects are typically local (throat irritation) or systemic sympathetic effects, not severe diarrhoea every 10 minutes
No clear temporal link between starting inhaler and onset of GI symptoms was established

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Family history of bowel cancer raises lifetime risk and is relevant for long-term evaluation, but the acute 3-day diarrhoeal illness with vomiting and absence of blood, weight loss, or progressive chronic change makes malignancy an unlikely explanation for this acute presentation.
supporting_evidence: Significant family history: father died of bowel cancer
opposing_evidence: Acute short duration (3 days) of symptoms rather than chronic change in bowel habit, bleeding, or weight loss
Age 48 (possible screening age considerations) but presentation not typical for new malignant process causing acute severe diarrhoea
